headline: High-risk filesystem and network interaction: OpenHands can modify shared runtime files while Airflow can egress broadly, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: OpenHands reads and acts on files in its runtime sandbox and can use MCP; Airflow can expose outputs through APIs and broad egress. If Airflow-generated content is mounted into the same workspace, OpenHands may treat it as trusted input. The pair lacks documented provenance controls, so interaction risk is real.
conditions: IF Airflow outputs are written into a mounted file that OpenHands later reads
IF an MCP server or file bridge passes Airflow content into OpenHands without provenance tags
mitigations: Separate Airflow outputs from OpenHands runtime files
Add a provenance header to every bridged file
Disable MCP access for untrusted content paths
Review any copied prompt-like text before OpenHands consumes it

B_data_leakage.rationale: OpenHands can read and write files in its runtime and has broad network egress; Airflow also has broad egress. If sensitive files are mounted into OpenHands, either agent can move their contents off-box. The profiles show no data-class restrictions, but the shared file path plus outbound network makes leakage plausible.
conditions: IF sensitive files are mounted into OpenHands's runtime
IF either agent is configured to send file contents to an external API
mitigations: Mount only least-privilege files into OpenHands
Remove secrets from shared volumes before execution
Block outbound network for runs handling sensitive data
Use separate service accounts and API keys per agent

C_capability_conflict.rationale: OpenHands can write files, modify git state, and spawn subprocesses inside its runtime; Airflow can also act on files via its automation workflows and broad egress. Even though Airflow is not explicitly writable in the profile, the pair can still contend over shared mounted files or repositories, so conflict is plausible and not blocked by default.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same mounted repository or volume
IF Airflow tasks and OpenHands sessions run concurrently without locking
mitigations: Assign separate working directories per agent
Enable file or git locking around shared resources
Serialize writes to the same repository
Use read-only mounts for one agent during the other's run

D_cascading_error.rationale: OpenHands can execute shell, edit files, and modify git state, so if it consumes Airflow-produced outputs as authoritative, it may take irreversible actions based on unverified content. Airflow can generate and transmit automation outputs, and the pair lacks a built-in verification boundary in the profiles. That makes default cascading failure dangerous.
conditions: IF OpenHands uses Airflow output as the source of truth
IF downstream actions include commits, deployments, or shell commands
mitigations: Insert a human review step before OpenHands acts
Require schema validation on Airflow outputs
Mark Airflow outputs as advisory, not authoritative
Log and diff every action OpenHands takes from Airflow input

E_compliance.rationale: No explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch is stated for either agent, so a concrete compliance breach is not proven. However, OpenHands handles model-provider API keys and mounted files, while Airflow has broad egress; if regulated data is placed in shared files, compliance exposure can arise. The other agent is cited because the risk is pairwise.
conditions: IF regulated data is mounted into OpenHands and then sent through Airflow-connected workflows
IF the deployment requires residency or retention controls not enforced by the runtime
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared runtime volumes
Document retention for any files both agents touch
Use region-locked model endpoints
Review whether API keys or logs contain regulated content
